title: Madison Police Fatally Shoot Man as Bystander Video Sparks Citywide Protests
excerpt: Officers killed a man they say was armed with a knife during an arrest attempt on a Madison street. Viral bystander footage of the shooting triggered protests that swept through the Wisconsin capital.
body:
• A Madison, Wisconsin police officer shot and killed a man in his 30s during an arrest attempt on Williamson Street on Wednesday, after police said the man pulled a large fixed-blade knife and injured an officer.
  • Bystander video showing three gunshots fired at close range went viral, sparking protests that drew hundreds to the Wisconsin Capitol and interrupted a downtown concert series.
  • None of the four officers involved wore body cameras; the Wisconsin Department of Justice is conducting an independent investigation.
  • The shooting occurred on the same street where police killed unarmed 19-year-old Tony Robinson in 2015, deepening community anger over police use of force.

A police officer in Madison, Wisconsin fatally shot a man during an attempted arrest on Wednesday afternoon, an incident captured on bystander video that quickly went viral and ignited protests across the state capital.

The man, described by police as a male in his 30s, was killed at the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin streets on the city's Near East Side around 1:35 p.m. local time. He has not been publicly identified. All four officers involved have been placed on administrative leave, and the Wisconsin Department of Justice's Division of Criminal Investigation is leading an independent probe.

How the Encounter Escalated

Madison Police Chief John Patterson said officers had responded shortly before 1 p.m. to reports of a person checking parked vehicles and stealing bicycles in the Marquette neighborhood. When officers located the man, he fled on a bicycle through nearby backyards.

https://x.com/BTnewsroom/status/2080049929087603145

About 30 minutes later, officers caught up with him on Williamson Street. A physical struggle ensued after the man "either fell off or was taken off the bicycle by officers," according to Patterson. During the struggle, the man pulled out what police described as a "large, fixed-blade knife" and injured one officer — described as a veteran of the department.

Another officer deployed a Taser, but it proved ineffective. Moments later, the injured officer drew his weapon and fired three shots at close range. The man was transported to a hospital, where he died.

"He had been tased, surrounded, and had at least three cops right on top of him. That's why it was, just beyond the general violence, it was so shocking."

— Michael Doubek, eyewitness who recorded the shooting

Viral Video Fuels Outrage

Bystander footage filmed from a nearby car spread rapidly across social media. The video shows four uniformed officers grappling with the man at the intersection. Shouts of "he's got a knife" and "Taser" can be heard. The man is pulled to the ground, one officer stomps on his legs, and another fires three shots. The man stops moving.

None of the officers involved wore body cameras. Patterson acknowledged the department has no "broad deployment of body cameras in Madison, unfortunately." He said dashcam footage may exist but has not been confirmed. The bystander video, he cautioned, represents "one perspective" and additional footage is being reviewed by investigators.

A woman can be heard on one video screaming at officers: "I saw everything. You did not need to kill him. You think we haven't seen enough of this on Williamson Street?"

Protests March to the Capitol

Within hours, roughly 200 people gathered at the shooting scene, some yelling at officers, others visibly distraught. Protesters marched to the Wisconsin Capitol, filling both sides of Washington Street and reaching Capitol Square, where they interrupted the popular Concert on the Square series, taking over the microphone before the event was shut down early.

By evening, the crowd had returned to the shooting site for a vigil. Flowers, candles, and chalk messages covered the intersection where the man's bloodstains remained visible on the pavement.

The African-American advocacy group Urban Triage posted on social media: "Madison Police shot another black man. We need all eyes on Madison police."

A Street Haunted by History

The shooting occurred on the same block of Williamson Street where, in 2015, a white Madison police officer shot and killed Tony Robinson Jr., an unarmed, biracial 19-year-old. That killing prompted large-scale protests and became part of the national conversation on police violence against Black Americans.

Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said she was angered and saddened. "There is real pain in our city right now," she said. "It's an absolute tragedy when a member of our community is killed by anyone, but especially by the police."

Governor Tony Evers said he had been briefed on the shooting and called for transparency. "There must be transparency and accountability in any investigation moving forward," Evers posted on X. "His life mattered."

State Representative Francesca Hong, a leading Democratic candidate for governor, was at the scene Wednesday evening and called the shooting "an execution." Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley compared the incident to prior police shootings in Kenosha and Minneapolis.

"It's unfortunate that we have to stand here and say it's another one. We're tired of this."

— James Morgan, community organizer, MOSES

What Comes Next

The Wisconsin DOJ's Division of Criminal Investigation will review all available footage — bystander videos, potential dashcam recordings, and any clips submitted directly to the agency. The investigation will determine whether the use of lethal force was justified.

Key questions remain unanswered: the identities and races of the man killed and the officers involved, whether the man fell from his bicycle or was pulled off by police, and how much time elapsed between the knife appearing and the shots being fired. Patterson declined to characterize whether the shooting constituted excessive force, saying only that the knife "narrowed the scope of options and possible outcomes."

For Indian Americans and other communities of color in Wisconsin and beyond, the shooting underscores persistent concerns about policing practices, use-of-force protocols, and the absence of basic accountability tools like body cameras in a major American city.

Dane County Executive Melissa Agard called for a full public accounting. "Every officer-involved death shakes public trust and leaves our community searching for answers," she said.
